episodes.213965: A strong cold front brought a smattering of thunderstorms through northeast Massachusetts, one of which caused a handful of wind damage reports in Middlesex county.
episodes.214221: Thunderstorms, fueled by MLCAPE values near 1000 J/KG, developed across the Mogollon Rim during the mid-afternoon hours. Under a northeasterly steering flow, these storms were directed southwestward, affecting most of Gila County before activity weakened as it descended into the lower elevations of south-central AZ due to weaker instability and decent convective inhibition. The cluster of storms that materialized across the higher terrain, however, did send a southwestward surging outflow boundary that traversed through the lower elevations of south-central AZ, producing gusty winds in excess of 30-40 mph and areas of blowing dust across the dust prone areas of Pinal County mostly. Additional clusters of thunderstorms did develop to southwest of the Phoenix metro, and although most of the activity was sub-severe with little to no impacts, a severe thunderstorm did develop across extreme southwest Maricopa County near the border with Yuma County to the south of Interstate 8 with a 73 mph peak gust measured by a mesonet station.
episodes.214313: Monsoon storms created heavy rain which produced flash flooding in parts of Arizona, including the Holbrook area.
episodes.214376: A stationary front, draped across the Mid-Atlantic, produced heavy rain and subsequent flash flooding across portions of New Jersey.
episodes.214713: An upper-level trough moved over west Texas and southeast New Mexico on the 16th. Dry air gave the region a brief lull on the 15th, but showers and thunderstorms developed once again on the 16th. Convection that developed produced heavy rainfall, and flash flooding was reported in numerous locations across the Permian Basin.
episodes.214774: The synoptic pattern shifted by mid July sufficiently to allow a more marked influx of monsoonal moisture into Utah. In addition to some isolated thunderstorm wind gusts, this resulted in numerous instances of flash flooding and debris flows.
episodes.214952: Multiple rounds of showers and thunderstorms produced several wind gusts in excess of 34 knots.
episodes.215259: A deep, tight closed low pressure system over the Olympics interacted with a very wet monsoon ridge. The region experienced unusually high precipitable water, and dew points in the fifties indicated that moisture was present through a deep layer of the atmosphere.
episodes.215260: A deep, tight closed low pressure system over the Olympics interacted with a very wet monsoon ridge. Unusually high precipitable water and dew points in the fifties indicated a moist layer throughout a deep part of the atmosphere. As the closed low migrated west, strong upper level support shifted into northwest Montana, generating severe overnight thunderstorms.
episodes.215287: A moderately unstable airmass underneath a closed, cool upper low allowed for the development of scattered showers and thunderstorms. A few of these storms were marginally severe in the Champlain Valley with strong winds.
episodes.215718: A strong upper-level ridge moved over the northern Great Plains allowing a moist, tropical airmass to move over South-Central Texas. Precipitable water values increased to greater than 2.0 inches which were near or above the 95th percentile of climatological values for this part of July. Multiple rounds of excessive rainfall were triggered by mid-level disturbances around the southern periphery of the high and low-level outflow boundaries. This convection was aided by nocturnal low-level jet streaks which led to slow moving, back building thunderstorms. Most of South-Central Texas received more than two inches of rain. The greatest totals were over Uvalde and Kinney Counties where 20-30 inches occurred. Another local maximum of 15-20 inches was observed in central Kerr County. Ten to 15 inches were widespread from Del Rio to Hondo and northward to northeastern Edwards to western Gillespie Counties. Damage estimates were near $115 million across South-Central Texas.
episodes.215942: A tropical upper tropospheric trough (TUTT) across south Florida on July 16th shifted northwestward and closed off into an upper low over the northeastern Gulf on July 17th. The combination of deep tropical moisture and mid level cooler air overspread into northern Florida and Georgia supporting numerous showers and thunderstorms each afternoon and evening developing along the inland-moving sea breezes. A broad surface low then developed under the upper low in the northeastern Gulf and gradually deepened into Invest 91 on July 18th and then strengthened into Tropical Depression 2 on July 19th. Showers and thunderstorms rotated around the eastern side of the system shifting northward up the Florida peninsula July 19th into July 20th. A few strong to severe storms developed as the outer rainbands from TD 2 interacted with the sea breeze and outflow boundaries. On July 20th, mid-level drier air filtered into the area from the south triggering some stronger downbursts.
episodes.216058: This was the first surge of deep monsoonal moist of the season, and the first and last with this intensity. The synoptic setup (Four Corners Subtropical High) in mid July brought a strong and deepening monsoonal moisture flux northward across Nevada, resulting in widespread deep convective with heavy rain, strong to severe wind gusts, and one convective event with a report of large hail. The monsoonal moisture surge led to deepening amounts of precipitable water from 7/15 to 7/19, PW was well above average.
episodes.216068: Had some reports of a half inch of water in one basement with flooding on Samuel Street.
episodes.216378: A cold front and strong upper level disturbance crossed the region through the morning into the afternoon of the 16th. Showers and thunderstorms accompanied these features. Some of the thunderstorms reached severe levels during the afternoon producing damaging wind gusts. The damaging wind gusts snapped or uprooted numerous trees along with broken branches. Trees and branches falling on power lines led to power outages. A brief waterspout also occurred. This was a low topped convective event characterized with low CAPE values along with high shear.
episodes.216501: Deep monsoonal moisture moved over Wyoming in the wake of the record heat wave. A strong thunderstorm developed to the east of Thermopolis and dropped approximately 4 inches of rain in an hour and a half. Warm Springs Creek overflowed and set a flash flood through ranches and into East Thermopolis.
episodes.216523: The region was along the edge of an area of high pressure from the 16th-18th. This positioning kept feeding in monsoonal moisture and instability to produce daily severe isolated severe thunderstorms to the region.
episodes.216786: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms in advance of a cold front moved offshore along the Downeast coast during the afternoon of the 16th. The thunderstorms produced strong damaging wind gusts while approaching the coast. The winds brought down trees and power lines at several locations along the coast including Blue Hill and Sorrento. Estimated wind gusts of 40 to 50 knots accompanied the line of thunderstorms crossing the coastal waters. A brief waterspout also occurred in Gouldsboro Bay.
episodes.216893: A slow moving storm system and abundant tropical moisture resulted in flash flooding across mainly the Northwest Hill Country and Northern Edwards Plateau.
episodes.216899: Upper level ridging was situated over the North-central Gulf during the afternoon hours of July 16th, while an upper low lingered across North-central Texas. Strong heating coupled with available moisture and the weak forcing along the east side of the low contributed to enough large scale forcing for isolated shower and thunderstorm development across portions of East Texas atop the upper ridge, with a small band of severe thunderstorms developing during the late afternoon hours across Upshur County Texas. These storms produced damaging winds that downed power lines near the Gilmer and Bettie communities, before diminishing during the early evening.
episodes.217117: An isolated thunderstorm passed over Lewis county on July 16.
episodes.217165: A slow moving front meandered over the region July 15 and 16 resulting in scattered storms that produced damaging winds, particularly over southeastern PA and South Jersey.
episodes.217263: Thunderstorms impacted south-central MT, producing gusts up to 65 mph and localized rain amounts up to 3 inches within a couple hours.
episodes.217266: A few storms impacted south-central MT, producing gusts up to 73 mph and hail up to 1.75 inches in diameter.
episodes.217296: Continuing an active monsoon period with heavy rainfall caused running washes and rivers that led to impassable roadways.  Additionally, there was 2 deaths in the Santa Cuz river due to drowning.
episodes.217349: Severe weather across Maine on July 16, 2026, was driven by fast-moving multicell thunderstorms and bowing linear segments that swept across central, eastern, and southern regions, resulting in widespread wind damage and major power disruptions.  An approaching surface cold front and associated mid-level shortwave trough moved southeastward out of Quebec and upper New England into Maine. Diurnal surface heating combined with boundary-layer dew points generated moderate Surface-Based CAPE. Moderate deep-layer shear fostered fast storm motion and cell consolidation into short bowing segments and squall lines, enhancing momentum transfer and supporting severe downburst activity.  In addition, a relatively dry sub-cloud layer and synoptical scale gradient alignment, helped faster even faster storm movement and DCAPE.  This lead to widespread damaging wind gusts, even with low top storms that didn't meet standard severe storm strength metrics.

Repeated heavy rainfall from recurring thunderstorms accumulated into a flood wave that moved downstream the Nueces River with rises near Crystal City beginning in the early morning hours of July 16 and cresting on July 17. Waters did not return to near pre-flood levels until about July 21.||Water began overtopping the Averhoff Reservoir dam early on July 16. Several water rescues occurred in the Crystal City area on July 17. Flooding spanned across extensive portions of FM1025 and the FM582 bridge. Over a hundred homes were damaged in the region. Flooding impacted the Chula Vista, primarily due to rises on the Espantosa Slough. Some homes experienced significant damage along FM65. Up to 3ft of inundation was reported at one home, with one eyewitness reporting floodwaters rising from ankle to waist height within 15 minutes. Some livestock were lost.||Across Zavala County, damage to public infrastructure reached $1.518 million. Countywide, 474 homes were affected by flooding, including 27 classified as destroyed, 156 classified as sustaining major damage, and 127 classified as sustaining minor damage, and 164 otherwise affected.
Thunderstorms produced locally heavy rain that led to flash flooding in Hunt. There were multiple water rescues in the town.

Multiple areas in Kerrville were affected. The Guadalupe River, Town Creek, and Quinlan Creek all overflowed their banks and flooded significant portions of Kerrville). Numerous water rescues and evacuations were conducted through the morning of July 16. Rescues mainly involved extracting people from vehicles driven into high-water areas. Many residences were evacuated in flood prone areas with floodwaters threatening. There were more than about 50 different evacuations of residences and apartment complexes. There was more than $55 million in damage to homes and infrastructure within the Kerrville city limits according to the assistant city manager. In August, the Kerrville mayor stated that damage to city infrastructure was estimated at a little under $100 million. Around $30 million of the damage was to the city���s water treatment plant, sewage lift stations, roads, and bridges. The combined public and private damage was estimated at $150 million for the county. FEMA reported 623 homes affected by flooding, with 7 destroyed, 131 with major damage, 373 with minor damage, and 111 others affected in some way. The city received at least 820 flood damage reports. The bridge leading from Junction Hwy to the Arcadia Loop area was partly washed out along Goat Creek, with the collapse of a 15-ft segment of the bridge. Buildings were observed floating onto the Arcadia Loop bridge. Most of Town Creek Road was either washed away or covered with debris. Large portions of the River Trail at Louise Hays Park were destroyed, heavily damaged, or covered in debris.  The Kerr County courthouse���s basement had at least 3-4 feet of floodwater with the county judge later reporting an estimate of ���as much as seven feet of water��� in the courthouse basement.

Slow moving thunderstorms produced torrential rain over southeastern Val Verde County near the Del Rio area early on July 16. Radar estimates indicated 3 to 11 inches of rain in southeastern Val Verde County with the heaviest amounts falling in rural portions of the county. CoCoRaHS observers recorded 4 to 6 inches of rain in Del Rio and the Del Rio International Airport recorded 4.72 inches of rain. San Felipe Creek swelled beyond its banks, reaching a crest of 16.99ft (6,010cfs) at 1000CST.||Flash flooding was reported by broadcast media in multiple locations in Del Rio, impacting low-water crossings. Seven water rescues and at least one report of floodwaters entering a residence were reported by local media. US90 was closed near Laughlin Air Force base due to flooding. The flooding in Val Verde County resulted in up to $2 million in damage to infrastructure.

Torrential rain from several slow-moving thunderstorms occurred along US90 in Kinney County on the morning of July 16. Rainfall totals across US90 were estimated to be above 8 inches with localized totals around 15 inches.||The flooding in Kinney County was one of the most significant in recent memory. Countywide, 80 total homes were flooded or otherwise affected, concentrated mainly in Brackettville and Fort Clark Springs. Of the 80 homes, at least 8 sustained major damage and at least 18 sustained minor damage. Water intrusion was reported to some classrooms on the Brackett ISD campus. All highways, farm-to-market, and ranch-to-market roads in the area were closed due to flooding, including US90 on both sides of Brackettville. Flooding occurred along Las Moras Creek along US90 and Gove St. Several roads sustained damage, including asphalt loss or damaged culverts. Washouts occurred on US90 at Pinto Creek. Flooding on Pinto Creek scoured out underlying portions of the RM2804 bridge. Lift stations were flooded. Evacuations occurred in Brackettville and Fort Clark Springs.||Damage to public infrastructure in Kinney County amounted to $2.8 million.

Comparison of high resolution satellite imagery taken on June 27 and July 27 indicates a narrow swath of vegetation damage near and along Shields Ranch/Phillips Rd and Ranch Creek southeast of Camp Wood. The damage swath was consistent and aligned with a weak tornadic debris signature observed on the morning of July 16 from the KDFX WSR-88D. Intermittent tree damage may have occurred farther to the northwest past the northwestern terminus of the defined satellite-observed data swath. This satellite analysis was corroborated with a report of damaged, broken, and mangled live oak canopy along the path at Shield Ranch. The EF0 intensity was assessed based on this report.

An off-duty NWS employee reported flash flooding in Gardendale. 0.8 inches of rain fell in approximately 15 minutes. The total time of occurrence is estimated from radar, and no damage was reported.
Power lines were blown down along Highway 271 south of Gilmer.
Broadcast media relayed a report of half dollar sized hail.
Multiple trees and wires were blown down across Barnegat Township.
Had some reports of a half inch of water in one basement with flooding on Samuel Street.

Report relayed via social media by a storm chaser.
Power lines were downed along Highway 155 northeast of Gilmer and east of Bettie.
Hail, up to 1.5 inches, was reported in the Pinewood Estates neighborhood.
Public report of flash flooding on Louisiana Avenue in Midland. The total time of occurrence is estimated from radar, and no damage was reported.
Broadcast media relayed a picture from the public of flash flooding in Monahans. The total time of occurrence is estimated from radar, and no damage was reported.

Broadcast media relayed a picture from the public of flash flooding at the intersection of Wadley and Ward in Midland. The total time of occurrence is estimated from radar, and no damage was reported.
A public report was received from an MPING of flash flooding on North Midland Drive. The total time of occurrence is estimated from radar, and no damage was reported.
Multiple trees and wires were blown down across Stafford Township.
Picture relayed on social media showed hail that was approximately half dollar size.
Widespread tree and wire damage was reported across Surf City.
Portions of Route 72 in Stafford Twp became impassable due to flash flooding. Some vehicles were disabled as a result.
Public report from MPING of flash flooding of streets and roads in West Odessa. The total time of occurrence is estimated from radar, and no damage was reported.

Video received via social media of muddy flows at Bald Mountain Pass. 1.81 inches of total rain fell at the nearby Bald Mountain Pass UDOT RWIS sensor, with 1.59 inches of rain falling in an hour. Time approximate.
Quarter sized hail reported by CoCoRaHS station NJ-OC-113 in Surf City.
An estimated 4 to 6 inches of water across Rochelle Road and Lower Elgin Road and was impassable.
A tree was blown down onto NJ 72.
HAM radio operator reported that the intersection of Highway 349 and CR 130 is  underwater. The total time of occurrence is estimated from radar, and no damage was reported.
The Iron County Emergency Manager shared a video of flash flooding on Kanarra Creek near Kanarra Falls.

A severe thunderstorm tracked across the Camas Prairie. At the Frei Hill mesonet, a wind gust of fifty-eight miles per hour was recorded at 4:30 PM PDT. Near Kamiah, social media reports indicated hail around one inch in diameter. In Harrisburg, hail was reported bouncing two feet off the ground between 5:07 PM and 5:14 PM PDT. The powerful hail and windstorm wiped out crops across nearly two thousand five hundred acres. Significant crop damage occurred to wheat fields between Cottonwood and Greencreek.
A severe thunderstorm produced quarter size hail at Aitken's gas station.
Delayed report of golf-ball size hail.
Hail up to an inch in diameter reported.
Sheriff reported downed tree 29.5 ft tall over State Highway 64. Time  estimated from radar.
Sheriff reported two ten inch diameter branches hanging on power lines.  Time estimated from radar.

A thunderstorm rapidly developed over Butte and moved into higher terrain northeast of the city. The storm dropped greater than half an inch of rain over upper Butte, leading to flooded streets including Silver Bow Boulevard and Harrison. Several public and media reports indicated hail up to one inch in diameter fell across the city.
Social media report with photo showing at least golf ball sized hail. Time estimated based on radar.

A severe thunderstorm moved through the Wise River area. A trained spotter reported half inch hail as the warning was issued. Radar estimates via MRMS indicated hail up to two inches in diameter. Public photos in Wise River showed massive hail up to two and a half inches across, roughly the size of tennis balls.

Local law enforcement officials along with UDOT cameras indicated a debris flow flash flood was reaching US-89 near mile marker 184. This debris flow originated from the Silver King burn scar at the outlet of Deer Creek.

South Turkey Creek Rd and Paradise-Portal Rd flooded. South Turkey Creek became bank to bank with 3 feet of water in it and flooding most of Turkey Creek Rd. Forest 42B Rd and  Portal Paradise Rd has flash flooding along the road.
